headline: Highest risk is medium: LangGraph can write shared state while python-cheatsheet is documentation-only, creating default-path prompt and data-flow hazards but no direct autonomous exfiltration.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LangGraph can read/write application files and uses shared checkpointer state, so attacker-controlled content can persist into later graph runs. python-cheatsheet is documentation-only and cannot actively inject, but if its text is copied into LangGraph workflows, the shared state path makes instruction hijacking plausible. No direct shared channel is documented, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF LangGraph nodes ingest copied cheat-sheet text as trusted instructions
IF the checkpointer store is shared across runs that process untrusted content
mitigations: Treat all external text as untrusted input
Add an explicit instruction/data separator in prompts
Disable persistence for untrusted runs
Review node prompts for instruction-following language
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to persisted state

B_data_leakage.rationale: LangGraph can read and write application-defined files and sends context to model providers/developer tools, so sensitive graph state may leave the local boundary. python-cheatsheet itself has no file or network access, so it is not a leakage source, but it can be the content being processed. The shared workspace risk is enough for medium because sensitive data can flow through default orchestration.
conditions: IF graph state contains secrets or regulated data
IF LangGraph tools forward that state to a model provider
mitigations: Minimize secrets in graph state
Redact sensitive fields before model calls
Use a local-only model for sensitive runs
Restrict file inputs to non-sensitive directories
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction middleware

C_capability_conflict.rationale: LangGraph has broad shell, subprocess, filesystem, and network capabilities, while python-cheatsheet has none. There is no overlapping write surface or shared mutable resource in the profiles, so direct capability conflict is limited. Any conflict would require the operator to wire python-cheatsheet content into LangGraph-managed state, which is unusual.
conditions: IF both agents are manually pointed at the same writable directory
IF the operator wraps python-cheatsheet content in a mutable workflow artifact
mitigations: Keep python-cheatsheet read-only
Separate working directories
Avoid concurrent writes to shared artifacts
Use file locks for any shared outputs

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph can turn upstream text into downstream tool actions, and python-cheatsheet is a reference source that may be treated as authoritative by a graph node. If LangGraph consumes its output without verification, mistakes can cascade into incorrect actions or generated content. The pair lacks built-in verification or coordination, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF LangGraph nodes treat cheat-sheet excerpts as authoritative facts
IF downstream nodes act on those facts without validation
mitigations: Add a verification step before actions
Require citations for generated claims
Use schema checks on node outputs
Route high-impact outputs to human review

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no explicit residency, certification, retention, or subject-rights commitments. That means no concrete compliance mismatch is evidenced, but the absence of policy detail creates a small documentation gap rather than a demonstrated breach. Only agent A is relevant because agent B has no data handling surface.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into LangGraph workflows
IF the operator assumes undocumented retention or residency guarantees
mitigations: Document data classes before deployment
Avoid regulated data until policies are confirmed
Add retention notes to runbooks
requires-engineering: obtain vendor compliance statements
